# filters.common { #wdm.filters.common }

`filters.common`

Shared filter types and numerical helpers.

The filters in this package are deliberately *generic*: they know about a
transition function, an observation matrix, and covariances, and nothing about
body weight. The model-specific wiring lives in `wdm.estimation`. This
separation is what lets the same unscented filter be tested against a linear
system with a known closed-form answer, which is the only honest way to be
confident it works.

## Classes

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [FilterResult](#wdm.filters.common.FilterResult) | Output of a forward filtering pass. |
| [GaussianState](#wdm.filters.common.GaussianState) | A Gaussian belief over the state. |
| [SmootherResult](#wdm.filters.common.SmootherResult) | Output of a Rauch-Tung-Striebel backward pass. |

### FilterResult { #wdm.filters.common.FilterResult }

```python
filters.common.FilterResult()
```

Output of a forward filtering pass.

#### Attributes {.doc-section .doc-section-attributes}

| Name                          | Type                   | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------------|------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| filtered_mean, filtered_cov   |                        | Belief at each step *after* incorporating that step's observation.                                                                                                                                                                    |
| predicted_mean, predicted_cov |                        | Belief at each step *before* the observation. Needed by the RTS smoother and for honest one-step-ahead diagnostics.                                                                                                                   |
| loglik                        | Float\[Array, \'\'\]   | Marginal log-likelihood of the observed data, accumulated via the prediction-error decomposition. This is the objective that parameter estimation maximizes, so its correctness is load-bearing.                                      |
| innovation, innovation_var    |                        | One-step-ahead residuals and their predicted variances. Standardised innovations should be white and unit-variance if the model is adequate; they are the primary diagnostic and the first place a misspecified noise model shows up. |
| observed                      | Float\[Array, \' t\'\] | Mask of which steps carried an observation.                                                                                                                                                                                           |

### GaussianState { #wdm.filters.common.GaussianState }

```python
filters.common.GaussianState()
```

A Gaussian belief over the state.

### SmootherResult { #wdm.filters.common.SmootherResult }

```python
filters.common.SmootherResult()
```

Output of a Rauch-Tung-Striebel backward pass.

The smoothed estimate at time ``k`` conditions on the *entire* record, past
and future. For reviewing history this is strictly the right thing to look
at: today's weigh-in genuinely does tell you something about last Tuesday's
true trend. For deciding what to eat tomorrow, only the filtered estimate at
the final step is available, since the future has not happened yet.

### gaussian_loglik { #wdm.filters.common.gaussian_loglik }

```python
filters.common.gaussian_loglik(residual, variance)
```

Log density of a scalar Gaussian residual.

### innovation_loglik { #wdm.filters.common.innovation_loglik }

```python
filters.common.innovation_loglik(residual, scale2, dof)
```

Log density of a scalar innovation: Student-t with squared scale ``scale2``.

``dof=None`` gives the Gaussian with variance ``scale2``. Otherwise the
innovation is treated as Student-t with the predicted innovation variance as
its squared scale, the same approximation the measurement update makes (see
`wdm.models.observation.student_t_inflation`).

### joseph_update { #wdm.filters.common.joseph_update }

```python
filters.common.joseph_update(p, k, h, r)
```

Joseph-form covariance update.

$$
P^+ = (I - KH) P (I - KH)^\top + K R K^\top
$$

Algebraically identical to the shorter $(I - KH)P$, but it stays
positive semi-definite under round-off because it is manifestly a sum of two
positive semi-definite terms. Over a few hundred steps the short form can
accumulate enough error to produce a negative variance, which then poisons
everything downstream. The extra matrix product is worth it.

### safe_cholesky { #wdm.filters.common.safe_cholesky }

```python
filters.common.safe_cholesky(p, jitter=JITTER)
```

Lower-triangular Cholesky factor, with symmetrization and jitter.

### symmetrise { #wdm.filters.common.symmetrise }

```python
filters.common.symmetrise(p)
```

Force exact symmetry.

Covariance updates are symmetric in exact arithmetic but drift in floating
point, and an asymmetric matrix will eventually fail Cholesky in a way whose
error message points nowhere useful. Cheap insurance, applied after every
covariance update.
